vignette: Arthur, a European-American psychologist, was fifty when he finally scheduled his intake, though the trajectory of his symptoms begins two years prior at a post-conference dinner. The event unfolded in a room heavy with the scent of spilled wine and peat whiskey, an olfactory density that seemed to seal the air around him. When the man's hands finally closed over his shoulders and pulled him to the floor, Arthur remained still, his body responding before his mind could catch up. Later, as he was carried out, the sharp wail of emergency sirens cut through the glass, a sound that would later lodge itself firmly in his awareness. What frightened him most was not the violation itself, but the sudden inability to name what had happened, as though the experience had slipped past his tongue and settled somewhere deeper, untouched by language. In the weeks that followed, Arthur noticed a persistent discomfort settling into his chest and jaw, a low-grade unease that never quite rose to panic but refused to leave. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, as if reaching for a thread in a tapestry only to have it fray before it surfaced. Often, the frightening event returned not as a picture, but as a heavy, wordless weight in his gut. He would sit in his consulting room, a psychologist accustomed to translating distress into language, and realize he could not seem to put the frightening event into words. The alcohol smell, familiar to most, became a specific trigger; one afternoon, when a visiting colleague entered his office wearing a sharp citrus cologne, the sharp whiff of ethanol in the hallway air made Arthur's breath shorten until he stepped back against his desk. Sirens on the street below similarly drew his attention, his gaze locked on the passing emergency vehicles until their passes grew routine. Emotional numbness followed quietly, a dulling that made his wife's questions at dinner sound distant, as though they were coming from another room. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. Sessions that once flowed with ease now felt like careful performances. He would watch his own hands on his desk and feel like an object, not like a person, observed rather than inhabiting his own skin. He continued his work, but the avoidance accumulated within the clinic's corridors: he stopped attending the Friday faculty meetings, delegated his supervisory responsibilities, and began leaving his practice an hour early. His wife noticed the change, not as a sudden withdrawal, but as a gradual settling into a quieter, more predictable pattern. Now, Arthur sits in his office, the familiar leather chair supporting a body that feels both solid and strangely detached. The discomfort has grown too constant. He is most afraid of the moment when he realizes he cannot remember the event fully, leaving him suspended in a half-recalled fear. He hopes that someone might help him find the words that have been waiting, so he might finally step back into his life rather than merely occupying it. His PCL-5 score rests at 53, a quiet number that maps onto the daily reality of a man learning to live with the weight of what he cannot yet say.
